query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for high-temperature applications, a synergistic interplay between the controlled, relatively slow outward diffusion of protective elements (especially aluminum and chromium) and a microstructure enriched in grain boundaries leads to the formation and retention of a continuous, adherent duplex oxide scale (for example, a Cr-rich outer oxide with internally dispersed Al2O3 or a CrTaO4-based oxide). This protective scale acts as an effective diffusion barrier to oxygen, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or conventionally processed high-entropy alloy containing multiple principal elements (including Al, Cr, and other refractory elements) with a coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition (increase or optimize Al and Cr contents) and process the material (e.g., via friction processing to refine the grain structure and increase grain-boundary density) to promote selective, controlled diffusion of protective species.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at high temperatures (around 1000–1100 °C) for extended durations (e.g., >100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The duplex oxide scale that forms—a dense, continuous, and adherent layer composed of a protective Cr-rich (or Cr-based complex such as CrTaO4) outer part combined with an internally distributed Al2O3 phase—mediates the improved oxidation resistance.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism is governed by the contrasting diffusion kinetics within the HEA: the inherently lower diffusivities of Al and Cr allow these elements to accumulate at the surface and form a stable protective oxide, while a refined microstructure (with increased grain-boundary area) accelerates the selective transportation of these species. This results in a continuous protective oxide layer that impedes oxygen ingress and further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline coarse-grained HEA with lower or non-optimized Al/Cr levels, the processed and compositionally tuned HEA will show lower mass gains, slower parabolic oxidation kinetics, and exhibit a thicker, more uniform, and more adherent protective oxide scale.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy having standard (or non-optimized) protective element concentration and a coarse-grained microstructure, which is expected to form less continuous or less adherent oxide scales and experience higher oxidation rates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is intended to apply to HEAs with similar multi-element chemistries under high-temperature, oxygen-rich environments (air at 1000–1100 °C for timescales on the order of 100 hours or more). It may not be applicable under low oxygen partial pressures or in environments where different oxidation mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the general roles of Al and Cr in forming protective oxides are supported, the quantitative contributions of diffusivity differences, the influence of minor alloying elements, and microstructural variances remain to be precisely delineated. The interplay between simultaneous nitridation or the formation of nonprotective oxides in certain compositional regimes adds further uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two variants of the HEA: one with an optimized high Al/Cr concentration and a refined microstructure (e.g., via friction processing) to increase the grain-boundary density, and a baseline variant with lower Al/Cr content and a coarse-grained structure. Subject both alloys to identical long-term isothermal oxidation tests at 1100 °C in air. Use techniques such as thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM)/EDS, and atom probe tomography (APT) to monitor oxide scale formation, composition, thickness, and mass gain.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (via cross-sectional SEM)
Phase identification in the oxide scale (via XRD)
Elemental diffusion profiles and grain-boundary hot-spots (via EDS/APT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized HEA does not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain, slower oxidation rate, or formation of a more continuous and adherent protective oxide scale compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesized mechanism—that selective, controlled outward diffusion of Al and Cr (facilitated by a refined microstructure) is key to forming a protective oxide layer—is falsified.

The initialisation and evolution of different oxide phases that were found with XRD scans agree well with these elements’ diffusion sequence order. Mn, Cr, and Fe preferentially diffused outward and became oxidized on the surface of specimens with time and temperature. The oxidation kinetics changed according to the content of Al initially from a parabolic (Mn15Al5) to a logarithmic (Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15) rate, caused by the formation of a protective layer of Al2O3 instead of the MnxOy oxidic layer observed in the case of the first-mentioned alloy. Moreover, the sub-surface oxidation and porosity caused by the Mn diffusion toward the oxide layer were completely suppressed from 10 at.% of Al, reducing the overall thickness of the oxide layer from ≈25 μm (Mn15Al5) down to ≈1 μm. Considering the above-stated, changing the content of Al can be used for precise tailoring of the complex performance of the prepared alloys to achieve desired properties not only at the laboratory but also at elevated temperatures.
